title: Every type of HSC equilibrium question, part 2: calculations
subtitle: You are given a calculation question you have not seen. How do you know which method to use, and where do students lose the answer?
subject: Chemistry
lessonIntent: Choose the method for an equilibrium calculation from what is given and what is asked, work through the five types (settled amounts, a start plus one settled value, K and a start with a tested shortcut, a mixture and K for direction, and an amount added), and name the classic slip on each.

voiceover.text: Almost every equilibrium calculation is one of five types: the three from the ICE table videos, and two more. What you are given, and what you are asked, tells you which. Settled amounts, and you want K. A start plus one settled value. K and a start, asking for the settled concentrations. A mixture and a K, asking which way it goes. Or an old equilibrium, something added, and a new value. We take them in turn, and spend longest on the last one, the hardest.

Type one: settled amounts. A two litre vessel holds 0.300 moles of sulfur dioxide, 0.150 of oxygen and 0.600 of sulfur trioxide. K uses concentrations, so divide by two first: 0.150, 0.0750 and 0.300 moles per litre. Write the expression with the coefficients as powers, not multipliers, and K is 0.300 squared, over the product of 0.150 squared and 0.0750, which is 53.3. Use moles and you get 26.7, which is wrong.

Type two: a start and one settled value. Put 0.400 moles of sulfur dioxide and 0.300 of oxygen in another two litre vessel, at a different temperature, and at equilibrium sulfur trioxide is 0.160 moles per litre. The start is 0.200 and 0.150 moles per litre. The measured 0.160 goes in the equilibrium row first, so sulfur trioxide's change is plus 0.160. Then the coefficients: sulfur dioxide falls 0.160 and oxygen falls half of that. The equilibrium row is 0.0400 and 0.0700, and only that row goes into K, giving 229.

Type three: K and a start, and you want the settled concentrations. You may use the quadratic formula, but an HSC question never needs it, so look for a perfect square or a tiny K. N two O four splits into two N O two, K is 4.0 times ten to the minus four, and the start is 0.500 moles per litre of N two O four, with no N O two. Which shortcut fits? Find the N O two. Pause here to answer.

If x of the N two O four splits, the N two O four left is 0.500 minus x and N O two is two x, so K is two x all squared, over 0.500 minus x. The bottom is not a square, so the square root will not help. But K is tiny next to the start, so drop the x: 0.500 minus x is about 0.500.

Four x squared over 0.500 is eight x squared, and that equals 4.0 times ten to the minus four. So x squared is 5.0 times ten to the minus five, and x is 0.0071. N O two is two x, which is 0.014. Test it: the amount taken off the start, 0.0071, is 1.4 per cent of 0.500, under about 5 per cent, so the shortcut holds.

A huge K is the mirror image. Start with sulfur trioxide alone, 0.400 moles per litre, where K for sulfur dioxide and oxygen making it is 4.0 times ten to the ten. Almost nothing splits, so let the oxygen be x. Sulfur dioxide is two x, and sulfur trioxide is about 0.400.
In K, 0.400 squared is 0.160, and 0.160 over four x cubed is 0.040 over x cubed. So x cubed is one times ten to the minus twelve, and x is one times ten to the minus four.

Test it: the amount taken off the start, two x, is 0.00020, a tiny part of 0.400. Now the other way round. If you started with just the reactants, in the ratio of the equation, and K was huge, nearly all of it would turn to products first, and you would take a small x back from there. An excess of one reactant would stay.

Type four: a mixture and a K, asked for a direction. Carbon, a solid in excess, sits with carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide. K is 1.90, carbon dioxide is 0.500 moles per litre and carbon monoxide is 0.800. Work out Q for this mixture. Which way will it run? Pause here to answer.

Leave the solid out. Q is 0.800 squared over 0.500, which is 1.28, below K. That is too little product, so the forward reaction wins and carbon monoxide builds up. Q chases K: below it, Q climbs. If carbon monoxide were 1.50 moles per litre, Q would be 4.50, above K, and it would run back.

Type five is the hardest: an amount added. Carbon monoxide and steam make carbon dioxide and hydrogen, K is 4.00, and a 2.00 litre vessel holds, at equilibrium, 0.400 moles of carbon monoxide, 0.400 of steam and 0.800 each of carbon dioxide and hydrogen. Steam is added, and the new equilibrium has 0.200 moles of carbon monoxide. How much steam was added? First convert to moles per litre: 0.200, 0.200, 0.400, 0.400. The new carbon monoxide is 0.100.

Right after the steam goes in, before anything reacts, the vessel is the old equilibrium plus the extra steam. So the unknown goes in the initial row: steam is the old 0.200 plus y, where y is the added steam in moles per litre. The new carbon monoxide, 0.100, goes in the equilibrium row first, so its change is 0.100 minus the old 0.200, which is minus 0.100, and the ratio is one to one all round. Steam also falls 0.100, because some of the added steam is used up, and the two products each rise 0.100.

At equilibrium that is 0.100, 0.100 plus y, 0.500 and 0.500. K has not changed, because the temperature has not: it is 4.00. So 0.500 times 0.500, all over 0.100 times the bracket 0.100 plus y, equals 4.00. Solve for y, in moles per litre. Pause here and try it.

The top is 0.250, so 0.100 plus y is 0.250 divided by the product of 4.00 and 0.100, which is 0.625, and y is 0.525 moles per litre. The vessel is 2.00 litres, so the steam added is 1.05 moles. Check: 0.250 divided by the product of 0.100 and 0.625 is 4.00. The slips: 0.525 on its own forgets the volume. 0.425 moles per litre forgets that some steam was used up.

Your turn, with a solid. Carbon, in excess, reacts with carbon dioxide to make carbon monoxide, and K is 0.400 at this temperature. In a 1.00 litre vessel at equilibrium, carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are each 0.400 moles per litre. Carbon dioxide is then added, and at the new equilibrium carbon monoxide is 0.500 moles per litre. How many moles of carbon dioxide were added? Pause here to answer.

The new carbon monoxide, 0.500, goes in the equilibrium row, so its change is 0.500 minus 0.400, which is plus 0.100. The equation makes two for each carbon dioxide, so 0.050 of carbon dioxide was used. The new carbon dioxide is 0.500 squared over 0.400, 0.625. That is 0.400 plus y minus 0.050, so y is 0.275 moles. A 0.225 answer forgot the carbon dioxide used up, and 0.325 did not halve the 0.100.

So read what you are given and what you are asked. Settled amounts: divide by the volume, find K. A start and one value: ICE table, with the measured value in the equilibrium row first. A start and a K, for concentrations: x, then a perfect square, or a tiny or huge K, and test any shortcut. A mixture and a K, for a direction: Q. An amount added: y in the initial row, K unchanged, answer in moles. Next: temperature and K.
